questions.prompt: Gram-Schmidt turns the columns of a full-column-rank matrix into orthonormal vectors. In the thin factorization \(A = QR\), those vectors and the coefficients that built them are stored as
options: orthonormal columns of \(Q\), and an upper-triangular \(R\) whose diagonal lengths are positive
orthonormal rows of \(R\), and a lower-triangular \(Q\)
the eigenvalues of \(A^T A\) on the diagonal of \(Q\)
a square orthogonal \(Q\) for every shape of \(A\), with \(R\) diagonal
questions.explanation: The prerequisite builds one orthonormal vector at a time and records a length and an inner-product coefficient at each step. Thin QR keeps the orthonormal vectors as the columns of \(Q\), so \(Q^T Q = I\), and it keeps the coefficients in an upper-triangular \(R\) with positive diagonal entries. \(R\) is not the orthogonal factor. Eigenvalues of \(A^T A\) are a different factorization. A thin \(Q\) is square only when \(A\) itself is square.

questions.prompt: Take \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 3 \\ 8 & 6 \end{bmatrix}\) and the thin QR with positive diagonal. What is the \((1,1)\) entry of \(R\)?
questions.explanation: Gram-Schmidt keeps the first column and records its length. \(\lVert(6,8)\rVert = \sqrt{36+64} = 10\), so \(R_{11} = 10\). The inner product of the two columns is \(6\cdot 3+8\cdot 6 = 66\), which is not a length. The second column has length \(\sqrt{9+36} = \sqrt{45}\), and that length is not \(R_{11}\).

questions.prompt: For a thin \(Q\) with more rows than columns and orthonormal columns, which matrix identity is the one Gram-Schmidt enforces?
options: \(Q Q^T = I\)
\(Q^T Q = I\)
\(R^T R = I\)
questions.explanation: Orthonormal columns mean each column has length 1 and distinct columns have inner product 0. Those are exactly the entries of \(Q^T Q\), so \(Q^T Q = I\). The product \(Q Q^T\) is the projection onto the column space, and it equals \(I\) only when the columns already span the whole row space. A zero product would say the columns are zero. \(R\) carries the lengths, so it is not orthogonal.

questions.figure_alt: A 2 by 2 matrix with columns (6, 8) and (3, 6).

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order that builds the thin QR of a 2-column matrix, with positive diagonal entries in \(R\).
questions.explanation: Each step uses the number the previous step just produced. The length has to exist before the division. The first Q column has to exist before its inner product with the second column. That inner product is the multiple that is subtracted, and only then does the remainder have a length. Swapping any adjacent pair uses a vector or a coefficient that has not been computed yet.

steps: Take the length of the first column and store that positive number as the (1,1) entry of R.
Divide the first column by that length. The result is the first column of Q.
Take the inner product of that Q column with the second column of A, and store it as the (1,2) entry of R.
Subtract that multiple of the Q column from the second column of A, and store the positive length of the remainder as the (2,2) entry of R.

questions.prompt: Continue the same factorization of \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 3 \\ 8 & 6 \end{bmatrix}\). The first column of \(Q\) is \((6,8)/10\). What is the \((1,2)\) entry of \(R\)?
questions.explanation: That entry is the inner product of the first Q column with the second column of \(A\). \((0.6)(3)+(0.8)(6) = 1.8+4.8 = 6.6\). The length 10 is \(R_{11}\), already used to build the unit vector. The second diagonal entry is the length of what remains after this multiple is removed, not the inner product itself.

questions.figure_alt: A 2 by 2 matrix with columns (6, 8) and (3, 6).

questions.prompt: Still for \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 3 \\ 8 & 6 \end{bmatrix}\) and a positive diagonal. After removing \(6.6\) times the first Q column from \((3,6)\), what is the \((2,2)\) entry of \(R\)?
questions.explanation: The remainder is \((3,6) - 6.6\cdot(0.6,0.8) = (-0.96, 0.72)\). Its length is \(\sqrt{0.96^2+0.72^2} = \sqrt{1.44} = 1.2\), and the positive-diagonal convention stores that length in \(R_{22}\). The signed first component \(-0.96\) is not a diagonal entry. Leaving the remainder un-normalized would store a vector, not the scalar \(R_{22}\).

questions.figure_alt: A 2 by 2 matrix with columns (6, 8) and (3, 6).

questions.prompt: Let \(a > 0\) and let \(b\) be a real number. The matrix \(\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ 0 & a \end{bmatrix}\) has the thin QR with positive diagonal. Write the sum of the squares of all four entries of \(R\), as an expression in a and b.
questions.explanation:
The first column is \((a,0)\), so \(R_{11} = a\) and the first Q column is \((1,0)\). Its inner product with \((b,a)\) is \(b\), and the remainder \((0,a)\) has length \(a\). Thus \(R = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ 0 & a \end{bmatrix}\), and the sum of squares of its entries is \(a^2+b^2+a^2\).
• \(a^2+b^2\) drops the second diagonal length.
• \(a+b\) adds entries instead of squaring them.
• \(2a+b\) is the sum of the first row, not the sum of squares.

questions.prompt: Once \(A = QR\) is known, with \(Q^T Q = I\) and \(R\) upper triangular and invertible, the least-squares minimizer of \(\lVert Ax-b\rVert\) is the solution of
options: \(R^T R x = b\)
\(R x = Q^T b\)
\(R x = Q b\)
questions.explanation: Substitute \(A = QR\) into the normal equations. \(A^T A = R^T Q^T Q R = R^T R\) and \(A^T b = R^T Q^T b\). Cancel the invertible \(R^T\) to get \(R x = Q^T b\). Using \(Qb\) forgets the transpose. Solving \(Qx = b\) asks the thin factor to hit \(b\) exactly, which a tall \(Q\) cannot do. \(R^T R x = b\) drops \(Q\) and also replaces \(A^T b\) by \(b\).

questions.prompt: Which statements are true of every thin QR factorization of a full-column-rank matrix, with the positive-diagonal convention?
options: The columns of \(Q\) are orthonormal.
\(R\) is square and upper triangular.
\(Q\) is square whenever \(A\) has more rows than columns.
The diagonal entries of \(R\) are positive.
questions.explanation: Full column rank lets Gram-Schmidt accept every column, so \(Q\) has one orthonormal column per column of \(A\) and \(R\) is square and upper triangular. The positive-length choice makes each diagonal entry of \(R\) positive. A thin \(Q\) has the same number of columns as \(A\), so it is not square when \(A\) is tall.

questions.figure_alt: A 2 by 2 matrix with columns (6, 8) and (3, 6).

questions.prompt: One step below is false. Select that step, and the reason it fails. The matrix is \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 3 \\ 8 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\), factored with a positive diagonal.
questions.explanation: The length 10 and the scaling that produces the first Q column are the opening Gram-Schmidt steps, and \(QR\) rebuilds \(A\) by construction. \(Q\) is 3 by 2, so its columns do not span every row direction. Orthonormal columns give \(Q^T Q = I\). The product \(QQ^T\) is the projection onto those columns, not the identity.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>tall matrix to factor</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">6   3</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">8   6</text><text x="98" y="114" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">0   0</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A 3 by 2 matrix with columns (6, 8, 0) and (3, 6, 0).
steps: The first column has length 10, so the (1,1) entry of R is 10.
Dividing that column by 10 produces the first column of Q.
Because Q is taller than it is wide, the product Q Q^T equals the identity.
The product of this Q and this R rebuilds A.
reasons: Orthonormal columns mean Q^T Q = I. The product Q Q^T is the identity only when those columns span every row direction.
The diagonal of R has to be negative, so the length step is the one that fails.
R is lower triangular, so Q R cannot rebuild A.

questions.prompt: Solve the least-squares problem for \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(b = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\) by a thin QR backsolve, or by the normal equations that the backsolve reproduces. What is the first coordinate of the minimizer?
questions.explanation: The columns are independent, so the minimizer is unique. \(A^T A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(A^T b = (1,1)\). The solution of \(2x_1+x_2 = 1\) and \(x_1+2x_2 = 1\) is \(x_1 = x_2 = 1/3\). A thin QR with positive diagonal produces the same point, because \(R x = Q^T b\) is the normal equation after canceling \(R^T\). The average of the three observations is \(2/3\), and that average is not a coefficient. The second standard-basis guess \((1,0)\) leaves a residual whose normal equation is not zero.

questions.figure_alt: A 3 by 2 matrix with rows (1, 0), (0, 1), and (1, 1).

questions.prompt: Why does the triangular backsolve \(R x = Q^T b\) avoid forming the Gram matrix \(A^T A\)?
options: Because \(R\) stores eigenvalues, and eigenvalues replace inner products.
Because \(Q\) is always square, so \(Q^T b\) is a copy of \(b\).
Because the normal matrix equals \(R^T R\), and a triangular \(R\) can be used directly.
Because the residual \(Ax-b\) is the zero vector for every \(b\).
questions.explanation: From \(A = QR\) and \(Q^T Q = I\), the Gram matrix is \(R^T R\) and the right-hand side is \(R^T Q^T b\). Canceling \(R^T\) leaves a triangular system. The diagonal of \(R\) holds column lengths from Gram-Schmidt, not eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix. A thin \(Q\) need not be square, so \(Q^T b\) is shorter than \(b\). A nonzero residual is the usual case; the backsolve does not require \(b\) to lie in the column space.
